lessons.title: How Quantum Computing Research Actually Gets Done

slots.practicalActivity: Based on this lesson's three research branches (theoretical, experimental/hardware, applied/software), identify which one is the realistic entry point for a self-taught software engineer with no physics degree, and describe, in the lesson's own terms, what kind of work they'd actually be doing there.
slots.deliverable: Your written identification of the realistic branch (applied/software research) plus a description of the actual day-to-day work in that branch, per the lesson.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply this lesson's 5-step repeatable reading pass to a real or recalled quantum computing paper (search arXiv's quant-ph category or use one you've encountered before): write down the claim in your own words from the abstract/intro, then check whether the results section's actual figures/tables support that full claim or a narrower version of it.
slots.deliverable: Your written notes following the 5-step reading pass on one paper, explicitly naming the gap (if any) between the claimed version and the shown version of the result.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite the vague research interest 'I want to know if a variational algorithm does better with more layers' into a testable, falsifiable hypothesis using this lesson's template, explicitly naming the specific technique, circuit/problem, hardware or simulator, comparison condition, and direction.
slots.deliverable: Your rewritten hypothesis statement with every blank of the lesson's template filled in specifically, not vaguely.

slots.practicalActivity: A student runs their novel error-mitigation technique once on IBM's cloud hardware this week, then compares the result to a baseline number quoted from a paper published two years ago on a different device. Identify at least two specific confounds this comparison fails to control for, and describe the controlled design you'd use instead.
slots.deliverable: Your written list of two specific confounds, plus your redesigned controlled experiment (control group, treatment group, interleaving, fixed conditions).

slots.practicalActivity: If the control group's measured probability had instead been 0.615 and the treatment group's 0.635 (a much smaller 0.02 difference than this lab's worked example), with the same 1,000 shots per condition, reason through whether you'd expect the z-score to cross the 1.96 significance threshold, using the lab's own two-proportion z-test formula.
slots.deliverable: Your written reasoning about how the smaller effect size interacts with the same shot count in the z-score formula, with a stated verdict on whether significance would likely be reached.

slots.practicalActivity: A student reruns a paper's exact published code and gets the exact published number. A second student independently implements the described method from scratch, using the same device, and gets a meaningfully different number. Determine what this combination of outcomes most likely points to, and which of reproducibility, replicability, or robustness failed.
slots.deliverable: Your written diagnosis naming which concept failed (replicability) and your reasoning for why the first student's success rules out certain explanations.

lessons.title: Selecting an Appropriate Paper to Reproduce

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lesson's screening checklist, evaluate two candidate papers — a 20-qubit proprietary-device paper with no code or data available, versus a 4-qubit open-hardware paper with a circuit diagram and parameters given in the text — and choose which you'd pick as your reproduction target, naming the two strongest reasons.
slots.deliverable: Your written screening comparison of both candidates against the checklist, plus your chosen target with two explicitly named reasons.

lessons.title: Extracting a Reproducible Methodology From a Paper

slots.practicalActivity: A paper you're extracting a methodology from states a circuit's gate sequence precisely, but never specifies how many shots were run per data point. Using this lesson's framework, decide whether that's a detail you can reasonably choose yourself and document, or a gap you should flag as potentially affecting the result, and justify your answer.
slots.deliverable: Your written classification (reasonable to choose vs. must-flag gap) with justification referencing the lesson's two categories of unspecified detail.

lessons.title: Handling Discrepancies Between Your Results & the Paper

slots.practicalActivity: You measure a result that differs from a paper's reported number by an amount that, per your own significance check, falls well within the overlapping confidence intervals of both measurements. Using this lesson's diagnostic checklist, determine whether this is evidence the paper's claim doesn't hold, state which diagnostic step this maps to, and write the honest conclusion.
slots.deliverable: Your written determination (this is not evidence against the paper) mapped to the specific checklist step (statistical noise), plus the honest conclusion statement.

slots.practicalActivity: If the paper in this lab's scenario had instead reported its 0.18 error reduction with a stated uncertainty of ±0.02, determine whether your measured 0.155 reduction would fall inside or outside that range, and state what that would change about the honest conclusion in your write-up.
slots.deliverable: Your computed range check (whether 0.155 falls inside 0.16-0.20) and your written revised conclusion reflecting that result.

slots.practicalActivity: You're choosing between reproducing a paper's error-mitigation result and extending it with one new comparison condition, versus designing an entirely new comparative benchmark from scratch with no existing paper to validate against. Using this lesson's reasoning about self-correcting project structure, write a recommendation for a first capstone at this stage.
slots.deliverable: Your written recommendation (reproduce + extend) with justification explicitly citing the self-correcting-project-structure argument.

slots.practicalActivity: Your own draft proposal's 'risks and fallback plan' section currently reads: 'The experiment might not work, in which case I will try something else.' Using this lesson's worked example as a model, rewrite this into a specific risk and a specific fallback for a topic of your choosing.
slots.deliverable: Your rewritten risks-and-fallback-plan section naming one specific risk and one specific, concrete fallback action.

lessons.title: Scoping a Capstone to Be Finishable

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lesson's time-cost categories (queue time, iteration count, write-up time), identify one specific way the Lesson 12 worked proposal's scope could still go over budget even with its stated fallback plan, and state exactly which cut-list step would absorb it.
slots.deliverable: Your written identification of one specific overrun risk and the cut-list step that would absorb it.

slots.practicalActivity: Explain why validating your zero-noise-extrapolation code against a simulator with a KNOWN injected noise model (where you can compute the true zero-noise answer yourself) gives you a stronger check than validating only on a noiseless simulator. State specifically what the noiseless-only check would fail to catch.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation naming the specific class of bug (errors in the noise-scaling/extrapolation logic itself) that only the injected-noise check can catch.

slots.practicalActivity: A device goes offline for scheduled maintenance halfway through your planned runs, forcing you to finish on a different (but same-model) device. Using this lesson's guidance, write what you should do about this in your run log and eventually your report, rather than just continuing as if nothing happened.
slots.deliverable: Your written plan for documenting the device switch, both in the run log entry format and in the eventual report's limitations section.

lessons.title: Capstone: Analyze Results Against the Hypothesis

slots.practicalActivity: Suppose the 5-qubit measured reduction had instead come out to 0.160 (slightly larger than the 3-qubit reduction of 0.155). Using this lesson's claim-by-claim framework, determine which specific claim from the original hypothesis this would contradict, and what the honest overall conclusion would be.
slots.deliverable: Your written claim-by-claim analysis identifying the contradicted claim (the relative-magnitude claim) and the honest overall conclusion.

slots.practicalActivity: In the worked diagnosis, the calibration-window gap was identified as the likely confound. If a re-run under a genuinely interleaved, same-calibration-window design still showed the 5-qubit reduction larger than the 3-qubit one, determine what the honest conclusion would become, and how it would differ from the conclusion reached in the worked example.
slots.deliverable: Your written revised conclusion for this scenario, explicitly contrasted against the original worked example's conclusion.

slots.practicalActivity: Your cut list and remaining time budget show you have enough time for exactly one more round of hardware runs before you must move to write-up. You have two candidate re-runs: the targeted, same-window retry, or adding a third qubit count 'just to see what happens.' Using this lesson's reasoning, choose which you'd pick and justify why.
slots.deliverable: Your written choice (the targeted re-run) with justification referencing the lesson's targeted-vs-open-ended re-run distinction.

slots.practicalActivity: Explain why this lesson recommends writing the confound/limitation notes down immediately at finalization time, rather than waiting until you sit down to write the full report. State specifically what would be lost by waiting.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation naming the specific details or exact language that would be lost by delaying the notes until report-writing time.

lessons.title: Writing Up Methods, Results, Limitations & Conclusions

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite the weak conclusion sentence 'Our experiment showed that error mitigation is a great technique for improving quantum results' to match this lesson's standard, using the actual numbers and scoped claims from the worked excerpt (0.155 reduction at 3 qubits, 0.120 at 5 qubits).
slots.deliverable: Your rewritten conclusion sentence using specific numbers and an explicitly scoped claim (naming the device, qubit counts, and calibration window).

slots.practicalActivity: A technical audience member asks: 'Why should I trust the corrected 5-qubit result over the original one?' Using the running capstone's actual calibration-window diagnosis and the worked presentation's approach of showing both results side by side, draft a concise, honest spoken answer.
slots.deliverable: Your written spoken-answer draft citing the calibration-window diagnosis and explaining the decision to present both results rather than hiding the original.

lessons.title: Presenting Quantum Results to a Non-Specialist Audience

slots.practicalActivity: Translate this technical sentence into plain, non-misleading language for a general audience: 'Richardson extrapolation across five noise-scaling factors estimated the zero-noise limit of the measured GHZ fidelity.' Keep the actual meaning intact — don't just delete the technical terms.
slots.deliverable: Your plain-language translation that preserves the technical meaning (what was measured, how, and why) without using unexplained jargon.

slots.practicalActivity: A visitor to your capstone repository has 90 seconds before deciding whether to read further. Using this lesson's README guidance, write the exact three sentences (the question investigated, the headline finding with its actual number, and the repo's organization) that should appear at the very top.
slots.deliverable: Your written three-sentence README opening covering the research question, the headline finding, and the repository's folder organization.

slots.practicalActivity: A reviewer tells you: 'Your conclusion says mitigation "significantly" helps, but I don't see a significance test anywhere in your results section.' Using this lesson's triage categories (must-fix, worth considering, noted but not changing), determine which category this comment belongs in, and state the specific action you should take.
slots.deliverable: Your written triage classification (must-fix) and the specific corrective action you would take in response.

lessons.title: The Real Quantum Computing Job Market Today

slots.practicalActivity: A job posting for 'Quantum Software Engineer' at a quantum-native hardware company requires hands-on Qiskit experience, asks for familiarity with at least one of Grover's algorithm or the quantum Fourier transform, and does not require a PhD. Based on this lesson, determine whether this is a realistic target for a strong portfolio from this path, and justify your answer.
slots.deliverable: Your written determination (a realistic target) with justification citing the lesson's two-tier distinction between software/algorithms roles and research/hardware roles.

lessons.title: Building a Quantum Computing Portfolio & Resume

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite this vague resume bullet into a specific one, using this lesson's standard and drawing on the running GHZ/ZNE capstone's actual project details (or your own capstone, if you've chosen one): 'Worked on quantum algorithms and did some research.'
slots.deliverable: Your rewritten, specific resume bullet naming the exact technique, result, and tools used, following the lesson's worked example's level of specificity.

lessons.title: What Graduate Study Adds for Research & Hardware Roles

slots.practicalActivity: Someone completing this 14-course path wants to become an independent quantum hardware research scientist leading their own experiments within two years, without further formal education. Based on this lesson, determine whether that's a realistic plan, and state what alternative destination might better fit their stated two-year timeline.
slots.deliverable: Your written assessment (not realistic without graduate study) plus your recommended alternative destination (the research-engineer or software/algorithms tier) with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: An interviewer asks you to walk through a project, and you're tempted to only describe the clean, corrected final result from the running GHZ/ZNE capstone, leaving out the original confounded runs entirely. Using this lesson's guidance, write out why including the confound-and-correction story is likely to make your answer stronger, not weaker, then write your own practiced 'walk me through a project' answer for your own capstone.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of why the confound story strengthens the interview answer, plus your own practiced project walkthrough answer.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student has completed the entire Quantum Computing Software Engineer path: they can read and critically evaluate a published quantum computing paper, form a testable hypothesis with proper controls, reproduce a real published result and honestly diagnose any discrepancy, and have carried one full original capstone project from proposal through build, unexpected results, analysis, write-up, and presentation — packaged as a portfolio-ready repository, with an honest, realistic understanding of which quantum computing job tiers that portfolio actually qualifies them for today.
